title: Welcome to Collinwood
full_review:
"Welcome to Collinwood" (Warner Bros.) visits a hardscrabble Cleveland neighborhood where a bunch of disorganized petty crooks think they can pull off a perfect crime. But since these guys can barely pull a wrapper off a stick of chewing gum, all goes awry in this passable crime comedy. It's like a Coen brothers film, but never quite as clever -- although it's also written and directed by two brothers, Joe and Anthony Russo.

When a lifer tells jailbird Cosimo (Luis Guzman) of an apartment safe with $300,000 in it just waiting to be cracked, Cosimo tells his girlfriend (Patricia Clarkson) to pay someone from the 'hood to do the time for him so he can make a beeline to the booty. At first she can't find a patsy, but the lowlifes she approaches all want in on the safecracking. Soon, aged Toto (Michael Jeter), ambitious Leon (Isaiah Washington), lonely Basil (Andrew Davoli) and baby-toting Riley (William H. Macy), whose wife is in jail and needs to pay a $1,000 fine to get out, all are looking for the patsy.

They turn to boxer Pero (Sam Rockwell), who pulls a fast one on Cosimo, getting all the details they need so the rest of them can do the crime while Cosimo's still doing the time.

Enter a wheelchair-bound former safecracker (George Clooney) who wants no part of this crowd but agrees to give them lessons in safecracking for a fast five hundred.

The plan is for Pero to romance the maid (Jennifer Esposito) from the apartment next door, get the keys and break though the wall to the apartment with the safe. Unexpectedly, love enters the equation, upsetting the apple cart. Pero falls for the maid and doesn't want to get her in trouble, while Basil wants to marry Leon's sister (Gabrielle Union) who will only have an honest man.

The fraternal filmmakers set a jaunty tone and the film makes the clueless characters into lovable losers. Hardened criminals they're not, though they don't stint on constant cursing or take a lot of interest in making an honest living. The visuals, dominated by shades of orange and amber, effectively capture the Collinwood neighborhood where the dreams may be big but the paychecks sure aren't. Loosely based on the 1958 minor classic, "Big Deal on Madonna Street," the plot falls into slim-pickings territory but the quirky characters are fleshed out rather divertingly. The ensemble cast works well together, no one trying to shine above the others -- including Clooney in what is basically an extended cameo.

The lapses in logic, how Pero gets put in the pen beside Cosimo, then is set free the moment he gets the info he needs, and why the incarcerated Cosimo's girlfriend is so anxious to marry this lowlife, are simply glossed over.

The movie meanders along with its comic complications, nicely buoyed by a music track that goes from polka to other ethnic selections.

Because of brief violence, recurring profanity, minor sexual innuendo, fleeting rear nudity and much rough language, the U.S. Conference of Catholic Bishops classification is A-III -- adults. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is R -- restricted.
